title: Francis Lawrence revisits Constantine's controversial R rating
excerpt:
Francis Lawrence recalls why Constantine received an R rating.
The director favors an adult-oriented approach to a potential sequel.
body_md:
Francis Lawrence still has unfinished business with the rating assigned to Constantine, his 2005 supernatural thriller starring Keanu Reeves. Speaking with Kevin McCarthy on the On Film podcast, the filmmaker revisited his unsuccessful efforts to secure a PG-13 classification and explained why the experience continues to frustrate him more than two decades later.

Lawrence's objection concerns the creative compromises made during production as much as the eventual restriction on audiences. He had deliberately worked within what he believed would be acceptable boundaries for a PG-13 release. Had he known that an R rating was unavoidable, he says, he would have approached the material differently from the beginning.

According to Lawrence, the ratings board considered the finished movie too intense and indicated that changes would not resolve its concerns. The director challenged that assessment by comparing the violence in Constantine with the battles depicted in The Lord of the Rings. The response he remembers focused on the distinction between fictional fantasy creatures and supernatural beings that some viewers believe actually exist.

That distinction surprised the filmmaker. It also illustrates how the perceived emotional impact and context of imagery can matter alongside the explicit content shown on screen. Lawrence's account describes a particular discussion from the original film's release period, however, rather than establishing a universal rule governing religious imagery in American cinema.

Constantine follows John Constantine, a troubled investigator whose encounters with supernatural forces place him between the human world and a conflict involving heaven and hell. Rachel Weisz co-stars in the film, which combines detective fiction, religious horror and comic book mythology. Its atmosphere distinguishes it from many conventional superhero adaptations, even though its central character originates in DC's publishing history.

The interview also offers a useful indication of Lawrence's preferred creative direction for a potential sequel. Having experienced the limitations of targeting a lower rating without ultimately receiving it, he would rather develop the next installment with an adult audience in mind. Such an approach could allow the filmmakers to embrace the horror elements more freely instead of attempting to anticipate the board's objections throughout production.

An R-rated sequel remains a creative ambition rather than a classification that has already been awarded. The available report does not establish a confirmed production start or release date for Constantine 2. Any eventual rating would depend on the completed film and the relevant classification process. For now, Lawrence's remarks explain why the original experience continues to influence his thinking about returning to the character.
